title: Read an Academic Passage — Learning from feedback
subtitle: Module 1
instructions: Choose the best answer using information in the text. You can revisit questions in this module until you submit it.
passage:
Feedback tells a learner something about a performance, but information alone does not guarantee improvement. A student may receive a detailed explanation and still repeat the same error if there is no opportunity to use the advice. For this reason, educational researchers distinguish between delivering feedback and designing a feedback process. The latter includes a task, information about the result and a later opportunity to act.
Consider an original classroom example. After a short presentation, students receive comments on how clearly they supported their main point. In one group, the comments are filed away before a new topic begins. In another, students revise the same presentation and explain which comment informed the revision. The second arrangement makes the use of feedback visible. It does not establish that every revision is better, but it allows the teacher to examine what changed.
Feedback also needs to be understandable. A technically correct comment may be too general to guide action. “Develop your argument” can mean little until linked to a specific unsupported claim. Conversely, correcting every detail may overwhelm a beginner. Effective feedback therefore depends on selection, explanation and timing, together with a learner who has a realistic chance to respond.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea?
answers: A feedback process requires opportunities to use advice.
questions.evidence: The passage distinguishes delivering information from a process that includes action.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes delivering information from a process that includes action.
options: A feedback process requires opportunities to use advice.
Teachers should stop giving written comments.
Every revised presentation is necessarily better.

questions.prompt: Why is the classroom example included?
answers: To illustrate different opportunities to apply feedback.
questions.evidence: One group revises using comments, while the other files them away.
questions.explanation: One group revises using comments, while the other files them away.
options: To prove comments should be private.
To illustrate different opportunities to apply feedback.
To show teachers cannot observe revisions.

questions.prompt: What does “the latter” refer to?
questions.evidence: The latter is the second of the two approaches named.
questions.explanation: The latter is the second of the two approaches named.

questions.prompt: Why might “Develop your argument” be unhelpful?
answers: It may be too general without a specific example.
questions.evidence: The phrase needs a link to a specific unsupported claim.
questions.explanation: The phrase needs a link to a specific unsupported claim.
options: It may be too general without a specific example.
It tells learners exactly what to change.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about correcting every detail?
answers: It can make advice difficult for a beginner to manage.
questions.evidence: The last paragraph says correcting everything may overwhelm a beginner.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says correcting everything may overwhelm a beginner.
options: It is always the best beginner strategy.
It can make advice difficult for a beginner to manage.
It removes the need for a later task.

title: Read an Academic Passage — Seed storage
subtitle: Module 2 · Foundation route
instructions: Choose the best answer using information in the text. You can revisit questions in this module until you submit it.
passage:
Seeds allow many plants to begin growing when conditions become suitable. A seed contains a young plant and a supply of stored material that supports its earliest development. However, keeping a seed alive for future use requires attention to storage conditions. Moisture and temperature can affect how long it remains capable of growing.
Seed collections are maintained for several reasons. A gardener may save seeds from a familiar vegetable, while a research collection may preserve a wide range of plant varieties. These purposes require records. Without information about where a sample came from, a collection of apparently similar seeds can lose much of its usefulness. Labels therefore belong to the scientific work, rather than being a minor administrative detail.
Not all seeds respond to storage in the same way. Conditions suitable for one kind may damage another. Collections test samples periodically to see whether they will still germinate, meaning begin to grow. A test uses only part of a sample so that the rest can remain available. Results help staff decide when fresh material is needed. Thus, successful storage is an ongoing process of monitoring and documentation, not simply a matter of putting seeds into a cupboard and leaving them there.

title: Read an Academic Passage — Measuring a proxy
subtitle: Module 2 · Challenge route
instructions: Choose the best answer using information in the text. You can revisit questions in this module until you submit it.
passage:
Researchers often measure something observable as a substitute, or proxy, for a quality that is difficult to observe directly. Library entrance counts, for example, may help describe use of a building. They do not by themselves reveal the quality of learning inside. A rise in visits could reflect a popular cafe, a longer opening schedule or improved study facilities. The number is real, but its interpretation depends on the question being asked.
A proxy can become particularly misleading when it becomes a target. Imagine a fictional programme judged entirely by the number of workshops delivered. Staff might divide one substantial session into several brief events, increasing the count without improving the experience. This does not mean that counts are worthless. It means that incentives can alter the relationship between a measure and the underlying goal.
One response is to combine evidence: attendance, participant accounts and examples of subsequent work may illuminate different aspects of an activity. Yet adding measures also adds effort and cannot remove every judgement. The strongest evaluation explains why each measure is relevant, how it may be distorted and which conclusions remain uncertain. Precision in reporting a number should therefore be accompanied by restraint in claiming what the number proves.
